This video offers an extremely rich soil worth tilling when it comes to cultural inquiry regarding the U.S., Canada, and rock and roll.

This is a Canadian band that came to the U.S. and mined its culture and history to present songs that told the tale of what it’s like to be an American better than the Americans could (with the possible exception of Robert Hunter’s writing for the Grateful Dead, their lyricist for a good portion of their catalog); reference Neil Young and Joni Mitchell, who were also Canadian, coming down to the U.S. and presenting musical offerings that far surpassed their American peers at the time. It is such an unlikely development in the history of rock and roll, this Canadian surge of high quality music coming into the U.S. at the time. This particular song puts you right at the crux of a crucial (albeit somewhat fictional moment) of U.S. history during the Civil War. And there are many other masterpieces on The Band’s first two albums. They changed over time, and “Cahoots” (esp because of the addition of a full horn section on tracks like “Life Is A Carnival,” another unarguable masterpiece) unfortunately did not have the beautiful innocence (without sacrificing wisdom) of the performances on their first two albums.

The change in character of the band members can similarly be tracked, and this is clearly evidenced in this video.

Levon Helm is in full command of his performance, but his delivery is far more passionate, almost strident, than the original studio recording of this song. It is arguable that this increase in passion, for perhaps the sole purpose of rendering a “driving performance,” lessens the lyrical heft of the song. That is why we turn back to the original recordings of these pieces, so many of them on the first two albums being worth their weight in gold: to receive the message(s) of their songs more clearly, not diluted by the almost overwhelming power of what The Band had become by the time The Last Waltz was performed and filmed.

There was a similar transition that the Grateful Dead went through. After they abandoned their massive, state-of-the-art sound system in favor of a stripped-down equipment line mainly featuring amps made by the then-emergent Mesa Boogie manufacturer, their sound was louder and punchier, but a certain grace, and most certainly many subtitles, were lost as a result.

I deeply love and admire The Band’s music. Although I turn to the Last Waltz videos for the pleasure of seeing the members delivering their performances visually, like BastionofFreeSpeech opined, I prefer the original recordings for their sanctity and pure vision.

One of the great, almost unknown secrets of The Band's music is the fact that Garth Hudson was the master architect behind their sound, especially in the beginning. If you tune into just the organ parts on the first two albums, you will soon discover what I am talking about. It was a much more subtle approach to rock ensemble arrangement than what keyboardists like Tony Banks (of Genesis) delivered (although Selling England By the Band is arguably an exception). It is sad and almost tragic that Garth Hudson is in a small, rather lousy old folks' home near Rhinebeck, NY. He does get to to play for "the public" there (his fellow seniors), but I doubt that very many of them or their visitors is cognizant of the enormous contributions Hudson made to the development of rock and roll in the U.S. I had a chance a few months ago to go pay my respects to Garth and am very sorry I didn't make the trip.
